svg.aria-label: Four real access-log lines, one per web attack - SQL injection, reflected cross-site scripting, path traversal, and file upload to web shell - each annotated with what its HTTP status code does and does not confirm
svg.title: Reading web attacks in the access log: SQLi, XSS, path traversal, and web shell
svg.text: FOUR WEB ATTACKS, READ FROM ONE LOG LINE EACH
SQL INJECTION — UNION-BASED
203.0.113.55 - - [20/Jul/2026:09:14:09] "GET /product?id=14' UNION SELECT username,password FROM users-- - HTTP/1.1" 200 9841
STATUS 200 + a response body roughly 15x larger than the baseline — the UNION column count lined up and the
query returned real rows. The same payload returning 500 minutes earlier just meant a wrong column count, not
a false alarm — it's still the attacker probing.
CROSS-SITE SCRIPTING — REFLECTED
198.51.100.23 - - [20/Jul/2026:10:02:31] "GET /search?q=<script>document.location='https://c0rp-status.net/c'</script> HTTP/1.1" 200 412
STATUS 200 only means the server responded — it does not confirm the script fired. Check whether the response
body reflects the tags unescaped; an app or WAF that HTML-encodes output still returns a clean 200 with the
payload sitting inert as text on the page.
PATH TRAVERSAL / LOCAL FILE INCLUSION
STATUS 200 with a body size matching a real system file is the read succeeding — an obfuscated ....// pattern
beat a filter that only stripped ../ literally. The identical request returning 403 a moment earlier meant a
control blocked it, not that nothing was attempted.
FILE UPLOAD TO WEB SHELL (T1505.003)
Both requests return 200 — the difference is what the request means. The POST just stored a file; the GET
carrying a cmd= parameter against that same file is remote command execution through it, running as whatever
low-privilege account the web server's own worker process uses — not SYSTEM or root.
READING STATUS CODES ACROSS AN ATTACK, NOT JUST ONE LINE
A storm of 500s or 403s from one source against one endpoint is still worth reading — it tells you the payload
shape the attacker was probing, not that nothing happened. The single 200 sitting inside that storm is usually
the request that worked — open that line first. And 200 is necessary but never sufficient on its own: for XSS
and web shells, always check the response body or the parameter, not just the code.
